title: 6 Simple Tips To Avoid Blundering Knight Forks (Remote Chess Academy)
text: The knight is one of the trickiest chess pieces, and its ability to execute the infamous knight fork makes it even more dangerous. In this lesson, I’m going to share 6 simple and practical tips that will help you avoid blundering knight forks—or counter it effectively if you’ve already fallen into one.

id: web:6 Simple Tips To Avoid Blundering Knight Forks (Remote Chess Academy):1
title: 6 Simple Tips To Avoid Blundering Knight Forks (Remote Chess Academy)
text: Here’s a quick list of the tips: Keep your pieces on opposite color squares; Maintain diagonal opposition against your opponent’s knight; Restrict your opponent’s knight; Prevent knight forks on f2/f7 and c2/c7 pawns; Put together a counter attack against a fork; Attack your opponent’s minor pieces.

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):2
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: A trapped piece is a piece that has no escape squares or squares where it can safely move without being captured. A trapped piece can be a bishop or a knight, but also ‘heavier’ pieces such as a rook or a queen can be ensnared. Even the king can be put into a position where it no way to move around. In the first part of his article GM Efstratios Grivas deals with a trapped king and trapped queens.

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):3
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: The following are the most typical means of trapping pieces: Capturing it!; Limiting its mobility using pawns/pieces and attacking it/locking it out of the game.; Chasing it to a bad square or corner of the board, where its mobility will be limited..

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):4
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: A trapped piece can be a bishop/knight, but also ‘heavier’ pieces as rook and queen.

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):5
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: Pawns are not referred to as trapped due to their limited movement, and kings cannot be captured, although any mate is essentially a trapped king!

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):6
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: Trapped pieces are important to recognise because they can often be won. We have to train on how to recognise and attack trapped pieces, but not all trapped pieces can be won easily.

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):7
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: If a trapped piece cannot be attacked or won, it can still be a liability, as technically material has been ‘won’.

id: web:Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase):8
title: Grivas on Trapping a Piece (ChessBase)
text: This is an often met concept, as we have many games where a queen acts carelessly and expose herself early in the game. In general, try not to move around with the queen in the opening, chasing ‘poisoned’ pawns!

id: web:The rule of the square (ChessBase Learn):9
title: The rule of the square (ChessBase Learn)
text: Think of a large square which is defined by the route the pawn takes to reach the promotion square. If the black king is inside that square it catches the pawn, otherwise it does not.

id: web:The rule of the square (ChessBase Learn):10
title: The rule of the square (ChessBase Learn)
text: The rule of the square allows you to know at once if a king can catch a passed pawn.

id: web:Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess):11
title: Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess)
text: In a previous article, the opposition was discussed. Like the principles in today’s article, the opposition often is relevant when there is a passed pawn. By definition, a passed pawn has no enemy pawns blocking its file or located on adjacent files. In an endgame with just kings and pawns, kings are often tasked with stopping passed pawns from promoting.

id: web:Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess):12
title: Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess)
text: Taking the opposition is one way for a defending king to stop the promotion of a passed pawn, but it is not the only way. Sometimes, a defending king may get inside the square of the pawn. A video, by International Master Andrey Ostrovskiy, explains the square of the pawn.

id: web:Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess):13
title: Chess Endgames: Pawn Principles (SparkChess)
text: The square of the pawn shows whether a defending king can capture a passed pawn, either as it races toward promotion or is on the promotion square. The square of the pawn is a faster alternative to calculating, “If my opponent moves their pawn, I move my king, they move their pawn, I move my king, they move their pawn” and so forth.

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):14
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: When we are attacking we are looking for one good option that will give us good chances of success. But when defending we have to find all the opponent’s ideas and adequate defence to each of them. It is for this reason defending is thought of as the most difficult chess skill to acquire.

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):15
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: Aagaard, in Attack & Defence, proposes the 4 pillars of defending against an attack:

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):16
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: Only Moves. When defending against an attack, it’s crucial to be able to find the viable □. Using the process of elimination and your imagination are essential here.

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):17
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: Comparison. Comparing different moves and variations with your calculation, visualisation and evaluation skills can help you find a path of survival.

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):18
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: Prophylaxis. You should ask yourself often, “what does my opponent want to do?” Aagaard believes “no one can come anywhere near their full potential without developing their prophylactic thinking.”

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):19
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: Active defence. In practice, your best course of action in most positions is playing actively, setting practical problems for your opponent. “There are times when a dubious-looking position can be saved with a perpetual check, forcing a drawable endgame or just by reacting actively to seemingly devastating threats.“

id: web:The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda):20
title: The 10 Things You Should Know About Defending Against An Attack In Chess (Junta Ikeda)
text: ‘What is my opponent going to do next?' Even if there is no direct threat, it is important to check his plans – whether they want to open a file, transfer the pieces, etc. It is already more difficult, but I insist you should consider this question BEFORE you consider what YOU want to do. Even though implementing your plans and preventing your opponent's plans sometimes come hand in hand, more often than not it is more important to pay attention to your opponent's plans BEFORE focusing solely on your own plans.
